meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Women want mediocre men, and men are working hard to be as mediocre as possible'?
meta.ogDescription: Attributed, not verified: the only citation on record is Quote magazine (15 June 1958). No Margaret Mead book has been shown to contain the sentence.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Credited to Mead almost everywhere, and there is one real citation behind it: Wikiquote ↗ lists the line among her sourced quotations and points to Quote magazine, 15 June 1958. That is a magazine reference rather than a page in one of her books, and no Mead-authored work has been shown to carry the sentence — so it stays attributed, not verified.

source.excerpt: Women want mediocre men, and men are working hard to be as mediocre as possible.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ places the sentence in its sourced list for Mead, giving it as the close of a longer passage and citing Quote magazine, 15 June 1958 — a magazine reference, not a page in one of her books.

Quote Investigator’s Margaret Mead file ↗ lists three investigations — the ‘healed femur’, ‘never doubt that a small group’, and ‘absolutely unique’ lines — and none of them is this one, so there is no specialist verdict to defer to.
The Quotations Page ↗ shows how the line usually travels: Mead’s name and dates, the verb changed to ‘become as mediocre as possible’, and no source given.
No page of a Mead-authored work has been shown to carry it. Her 1949 study of the sexes, Male and Female ↗, is the natural place to look and is not documented as the source.
source.excerptNote: Wikiquote prints this sentence as the close of a longer Mead passage contrasting societies fascinated by inner life with societies fixed on what can be built, altered and invented. The closing sentence is the part that travels on its own, and it is the only part the quote sites carry.

source.rightsNote: Every candidate source for this sentence falls well after the 1931 US public-domain cutoff: the only citation on record is a magazine dated 15 June 1958, and Mead’s 1949 study of the sexes ↗ was published by William Morrow. Mead died in 1978 and her writing remains under copyright, so the line should be treated as in-copyright and quoted only briefly, with attribution.

author.name: Margaret Mead
author.heading: Who Margaret Mead actually was
author.metaLine: 1901–1978 · American cultural anthropologist and public intellectual
author.bio: Margaret Mead was the American cultural anthropologist who made the discipline a household word, first with Coming of Age in Samoa (1928) and then across a half-century of fieldwork, museum work and popular writing. She served as curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History and, later, as president of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, while co-writing a monthly Redbook column that put her opinions on marriage, sex and family in front of a mass audience. That last role is exactly why quotations attach to her so easily: she published constantly in popular magazines, which makes almost any brisk line about men and women sound plausible in her voice.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: No rival author is claiming this sentence — the trouble is the wording, which drifts, and the paper trail, which is one line long.

items.who: “…working hard to become as mediocre as possible”
items.why: The verb is not stable in circulation. The Quotations Page ↗ prints “working hard to become as mediocre as possible,” where Wikiquote ↗ has “working hard to be as mediocre as possible.” A one-word difference is a reliable sign a line has been passed hand to hand rather than copied off a page.

The quote-site layer gives no citation at all — The Quotations Page ↗ offers her name, her dates and a bookseller link. Readers then supply a source themselves, usually one of her famous books; the article on Male and Female (1949) ↗, the obvious candidate, does not quote it.

It is worth saying plainly that the specialists have not ruled here. QI’s Margaret Mead category ↗ holds three investigations and this is not one of them, so anyone asserting a confident origin is going beyond the published research.

misattribution.truthLine: The single citation anyone has attached to this sentence is the one at Wikiquote ↗: Quote magazine, 15 June 1958. Until that issue is read page by page, “attributed to Margaret Mead” is exactly as far as the evidence reaches.

context.heading: Why it sounds exactly like her
lead: Mead was the rare anthropologist the general public actually read, and by 1949 she was writing head-on about the sexes: Male and Female: A Study of the Sexes in a Changing World, published by William Morrow, set men and women across seven Pacific societies beside men and women in the United States. Aeon’s survey of her career notes that the book struck many readers as a reversal — where Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935) had argued gender roles were largely cultural, Male and Female leaned much harder on biology (Aeon ↗).

That is the register this sentence lives in: brisk, faintly acid, aimed at American mating habits rather than at Samoa. It is also why it passes so easily as hers. But sounding like Mead is not the same as being traceable to Mead — and here the trail runs out at a single 1958 magazine reference.
detailsBody: Two checks that could have moved it up both came back empty. Quote Investigator has published three Margaret Mead investigations — the ‘healed femur’ line, ‘never doubt that a small group of thoughtful, committed citizens’, and ‘you are absolutely unique’ — and none of them is this one (QI’s Mead file ↗), so there is no specialist finding to adopt.

The aggregator layer supplies nothing either. The Quotations Page gives Mead’s name and life dates, a slightly different verb, and no citation whatsoever (entry ↗). Wikiquote’s 1958 magazine reference is the only pointer to a physical page anywhere in the chain, and until that issue is read the sentence cannot honestly be called verified.
context.pull: Sounding like Mead is not the same as being traceable to Mead.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Women want mediocre men, and men are working hard to be as mediocre as possible" in its sourced section for Margaret Mead, as the close of a longer passage, with the citation Quote magazine (15 June 1958).
Quote Investigator's Margaret Mead category contains only three investigations (healed femur; never doubt that a small group; absolutely unique) and none about "mediocre men".
A Quote Investigator site search for "mediocre men" returns no article about this quotation or about Margaret Mead.
The Quotations Page attributes the variant wording "working hard to become as mediocre as possible" to Margaret Mead with her life dates and no source citation.

Margaret Mead lived 16 December 1901 to 15 November 1978, was an American cultural anthropologist and public intellectual, curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History, and wrote a monthly Redbook column.

Male and Female: A Study of the Sexes in a Changing World was published by William Morrow and Company in 1949 and compares men and women on seven Pacific islands with men and women in the United States; the article does not contain the phrase "women want mediocre men".

Aeon's essay discusses the apparent reversal between Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935) and Male and Female (1949), which leaned more on biological difference, and does not contain the phrase "women want mediocre men".
